blocks.instruction: Leia o texto e escolha a alternativa correta. Algumas perguntas pedem inferência — a resposta não está escrita com todas as letras.
blocks.passage:
At senior level, contract work is less about drafting and more about discipline. The question is not "what does this clause say?" but "what would this clause do if every possible thing went wrong?" Senior lawyers and senior trade executives read every contract twice: once for the deal as imagined, and once for the deal as feared.

The discipline rests on three habits. First, drafting that says what it means — plain, specific, and as short as the law allows; every ambiguous phrase is a future dispute postponed, not avoided. Second, clauses that survive a change of personnel — the contract must still make sense when the people who drafted it have moved on. Third, explicit ownership of risk: who bears what, measured in time, money and jurisdiction.

Contractual English at this level uses shall, may, must, is entitled to, shall not unreasonably withhold, and notwithstanding the foregoing — not to sound formal, but because each of these carries a very precise legal weight. Using them correctly is part of the craft. Using them carelessly is a quiet way to lose a case that had not even begun.

items.q: According to the text, at senior level contract work is mainly about…
items.why: "contract work is less about drafting and more about discipline".

items.q: Why do senior professionals read every contract twice?
options: To check the spelling and formatting
Once for the deal as imagined and once for the deal as feared
Once for each party to the agreement
To compare it against previous versions
items.why: "once for the deal as imagined, and once for the deal as feared."

items.q: What does the text say an ambiguous phrase really is?
options: A future dispute postponed, not avoided
A matter for the courts alone
items.why: "every ambiguous phrase is a future dispute postponed, not avoided."

items.q: Which statement would the author most likely DISAGREE with?
options: Formal legal words carry precise legal weight.
A contract should still make sense after its drafters have left.
Long, elaborate wording is what gives a clause its strength.
Clarity is a discipline, not merely a matter of taste.
items.why: Inferência: o texto diz que o peso vem da escolha da palavra, não do tamanho — "as short as the law allows".

items.q: The phrase "a quiet way to lose a case that had not even begun" suggests that…
options: careless wording creates risk long before any dispute is filed
most cases are won before they reach court
cases should be settled early to save money
items.why: Inferência: um modal usado sem cuidado já semeia a derrota — o dano é anterior ao litígio.

blocks.instruction: Ouça Charlotte conduzindo a revisão jurídica final, cláusula por cláusula. Responda sem ler a transcrição — ela só aparece depois de corrigir.

audio.text:
Right, let's take this line by line — I'd rather we lose an hour now than a year in arbitration later. Start at clause fourteen.

It says the supplier "shall use reasonable endeavours" to meet the delivery window. That's soft. If this volume matters as much as the commercial team says it does, "shall use reasonable endeavours" gives us almost nothing to enforce. I'd want "shall deliver by", with a defined remedy if they don't. Let's not confuse an obligation with a good intention.

Clause twenty-two — consent "shall not be unreasonably withheld". Fine, but who decides what is unreasonable, and under which jurisdiction? Right now that's ambiguous, and ambiguous is expensive. Pin it down.

And I noticed a "notwithstanding the foregoing" in the indemnity section that quietly overrides the liability cap two pages earlier. Whoever drafted that may not have intended it, but as written, it does. That one word could cost us the entire ceiling on our exposure.

So: plain language, explicit ownership of risk, and a contract that still reads correctly when none of us are in the room. Send me the redline by Thursday.
audio.label: Ouça quantas vezes precisar. A transcrição aparece depois de corrigir.

items.q: Why does Charlotte object to "shall use reasonable endeavours" in clause fourteen?
options: It is too soft to enforce for a volume that matters
It appears twice in the contract
items.why: "That's soft… gives us almost nothing to enforce." Ela prefere "shall deliver by" com remédio definido.

items.q: What is Charlotte's concern about "shall not be unreasonably withheld" in clause twenty-two?
options: The consent should never be withheld
It is unclear who decides what is unreasonable, and under which jurisdiction
items.why: "who decides what is unreasonable, and under which jurisdiction? … ambiguous is expensive."

items.q: What problem does the "notwithstanding the foregoing" create in the indemnity section?
options: It quietly overrides the liability cap set two pages earlier
items.why: "a 'notwithstanding the foregoing'… quietly overrides the liability cap two pages earlier."

items.q: When Charlotte says "Let's not confuse an obligation with a good intention," she implies that…
options: the supplier is acting in bad faith
wording that merely signals effort does not bind the way a firm duty does
the commercial team is overstating the volume
good intentions are enough in long-term deals
items.why: Inferência: "reasonable endeavours" é intenção; "shall deliver by" é obrigação exigível.

items.q: What does Charlotte's remark that she'd "rather lose an hour now than a year in arbitration later" reveal about her approach?
options: She is reluctant to spend time on the review
She treats meticulous review now as cheaper than disputes later
She expects the deal to collapse
items.why: Inferência: o rigor antecipado é a economia — evitar o litígio caro depois.

blocks.instruction: O vocabulário da lição aparece aqui em frases novas. Escolha o sentido ou a palavra que cabe no contexto.

items.q: "The clause was hopelessly ambiguous, so each side read it in its own favour." Ambiguous means…
options: open to more than one interpretation
items.why: Ambiguous = ambíguo: aberto a mais de uma leitura.

items.q: Choose the correct word: "Under this clause the buyer is ___ a full refund if delivery is late."
items.why: "Is entitled to" = com direito a — confere um direito, não uma obrigação.

items.q: "Consent shall not be unreasonably withheld." Unreasonably means the consent may be refused only…
items.why: Unreasonably = injustificadamente; portanto só se pode recusar com motivo razoável.

items.q: "Notwithstanding the foregoing, the liability cap shall remain fixed." This phrase signals that the sentence…
options: overrides whatever was stated before it
items.why: Notwithstanding the foregoing = não obstante o acima mencionado — prevalece sobre o que veio antes.

items.q: "Precise drafting is a craft, learned over years at the negotiating table." A craft is…
options: a skilled trade mastered through practice
items.why: Craft = ofício: habilidade apurada com prática.

blocks.instruction: Expressões e phrasal verbs que aparecem em revisões contratuais. Escolha o sentido no contexto.

items.q: "The general counsel still has to sign off on the indemnity clause." To sign off on means to…
items.why: Sign off on = aprovar formalmente, dar o aval final.

items.q: "Two of the regional heads pushed back on the liability cap." They…
items.why: Push back on = resistir, discordar — sem necessariamente rejeitar de vez.

items.q: "We agreed the remedy but never followed through on the wording." They…
options: failed to carry it to completion
items.why: Follow through = levar até o fim o que foi combinado.

items.q: "Let's iron out the ambiguity in clause twenty-two before we send the redline." To iron out means to…
options: resolve or smooth away a problem
items.why: Iron out = aparar arestas, resolver um ponto problemático.

items.q: "That single word could expose us to unlimited liability." To expose someone to a risk means to…
options: cap it at a fixed amount
items.why: Expose (someone) to = deixar sujeito, vulnerável a um risco.
